Abbie Hoffman (November 30, 1936 - April 12, 1989) was an American political and social activist who co-founded the Youth International Party ("Yippies") and was a member of the Chicago Seven.

This Russian chess grandmaster reigned as the 12th World Chess Champion from 1975 to 1985, later adding three more FIDE World Championship titles in the 1990s — who is he?
Anatoly Karpov (born May 23, 1951) is a Russian and former Soviet chess grandmaster, former World Chess Champion, and politician.

Borrowed from a Sanskrit word, this term originated as the ethno-cultural self-designation of ancient Indo-Iranian peoples, used both in Vedic India and, per the Avesta, among ancient Iranian peoples to describe themselves — name the term?
Aryan (borrowed from Sanskrit rya), is a term originating from the ethno-cultural self-designation of the Indo-Iranians.
In 751, an Abbasid-Tibetan force defeated Tang China's army for control of territory near the Syr Darya, ending Tang expansion into Central Asia — which clash?
Battle of Talas (pinyin: Dlus Zhny) was an armed confrontation between the Abbasid Caliphate along with the Tibetan Empire against the Tang dynasty and its allies in 751.
According to the Book of Genesis, Abraham was commanded to perform this covenant rite on a baby boy's eighth day of life, traditionally carried out by a mohel — what is it called?
Brit milah ("covenant of circumcision"), or bris, is the ceremony of circumcision in Judaism and Samaritanism during which a newborn male's foreskin is surgically removed.
Said to hail from Lycia in Asia Minor, this fire-breathing Greek monster is typically depicted as a lion with a goat's head sprouting from its back and a snake for a tail — what is it?
Chimera (mythology) (ky-MEER-ə, kih-, -MAIR-ə; lit. 'she-goat') was a monstrous fire-breathing hybrid creature in Greek mythology.

Daniel Boone was American pioneer and frontiersman (1734–1820).
The first president of India born in the independent nation, and only the second woman to hold the role — which former governor of Jharkhand took office in 2022?
Droupadi Murmu (born Durgi Tudu; 20 June 1958) is an Indian politician who has served as the president of India since 2022.
Fill in the blank: “____ (15 February 1949 - 22 October 1988) was a Turkish military officer who was appointed governor of the Diyarbakr Prison after the 1980 Turkish coup d'tat.”

Esat Oktay Yıldıran (15 February 1949 - 22 October 1988) was a Turkish military officer who was appointed governor of the Diyarbakr Prison after the 1980 Turkish coup d'tat. During the PKK insurgency, Yıldıran became known for his extensive torture of PKK aligned Kurds in the Diyarbakır Prison.

Beginning with the Estates General in 1789, this period of political and societal upheaval in France ended with the Coup of 18 Brumaire and established principles central to liberal democracy. What was it?
French Revolution was a period of political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789 and ended with the Coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799.

Born in Kiev and raised in Milwaukee, where she trained as a teacher and embraced Labor Zionism, this future leader emigrated to Mandatory Palestine in 1921 and became her nation's first and only female head of government. Who was she?
Golda Meir (previously Meyerson; ne Mabovitch; 3 May 1898 - 8 December 1978) was the prime minister of Israel from 1969 to 1974.

This Sunni Islamist paramilitary group, born from a January 2017 merger of several Syrian rebel factions, spearheaded the offensive that ended over 13 years of civil war in December 2024 — which group?
Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) was a Sunni Islamist political organisation and paramilitary group involved in the Syrian civil war.
A former police chief who once led Taiwan's National Police Agency, this politician became mayor of New Taipei and ran as the Kuomintang's candidate in the 2024 presidential election — who is he?
Hou Yu-ih (pinyin: Hu Yuy; born 7 June 1957) is a Taiwanese politician, criminologist, and former police officer who has served as the mayor of New Taipei since 25 December 2018.
The only queen to reign in her own right over a unified Spain, this monarch took the throne a month before her third birthday in 1833 and was deposed in 1868 — who was she?
Isabella II (10 October 1830 - 9 April 1904) was Queen of Spain from 1833 until her deposition in 1868.

Elected New York's first female county judge and later county district attorney, this Lebanese-American TV host and lawyer has served as the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia since May 2025. Who is she?
Jeanine Pirro (born June 2, 1951) is a Lebanese-American television host, lawyer, and author who has been serving as the United States attorney for the District of Columbia since May 2025.

Joseph of Arimathea (Ancient) is a Biblical figure who assumed responsibility for the burial of Jesus after his crucifixion.
This Emirati government official and business leader has served on Abu Dhabi's Executive Council since 2006, and has also acted as the UAE's Presidential Special Envoy to China since 2018. Who is he?
Khaldoon Al Mubarak (born 27 January 1976) is an Emirati government official and business leader.

Raised under Japanese rule and trained as an agricultural economist with a Cornell doctorate, he became the first president of the Republic of China born in Taiwan — and its first directly elected one. Who was he?

Lee Teng-hui (pinyin: L Dnghu; 15 January 1923 - 30 July 2020) was a Taiwanese statesman, economist, and agronomist who served as the fourth president of the Republic of China and chairman of the Kuomintang from 1988 to 2000.
This ancient Indian kingdom on the eastern Ganges Plain formed the core of the Mauryan and Gupta Empires and played a key role in the early development of Jainism and Buddhism — what was it called?
Magadha was a region and kingdom in ancient India, based in the eastern Ganges Plain.
Born in 1946, which longtime Kurdistan Democratic Party leader governed as President of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq for over a decade starting in 2005?

Masoud Barzani (born 16 August 1946) is a Kurdish politician who has been leader of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) since 1979, and was President of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq from 2005 to 2017.
This jurist served two terms as president of Georgia, founded its United National Movement party, and later became governor of Ukraine's Odesa Oblast — who is he?
Mikheil Saakashvili (born 21 December 1967) is a Georgian-Ukrainian politician.
Captured during an intelligence mission in New York and executed by the British in 1776, this Continental Army officer was named Connecticut's state hero in 1985 — who is he?
Nathan Hale (June 6, 1755 - September 22, 1776) was an American Patriot, soldier, and spy for the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War.
The younger sister of unifier Oda Nobunaga, this Sengoku-era noblewoman became the mother of three daughters who each grew into prominent figures in their own right — who was she?
Oichi (1547 - June 14, 1583) was a female historical figure in the late Sengoku period.
A Spanish politician and economist who has served as Prime Minister of Spain since 2018 and as Secretary-General of the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party. Who is he?
Pedro Sánchez (born 29 February 1972) is a Spanish politician and economist who has served as Prime Minister of Spain since 2018.
This anthology of ancient Hebrew religious hymns, found in the Ketuvim section of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally comprises 150 individual pieces. What is it?

Founder of the System Capital Management investment group, this billionaire is both Ukraine's richest man and the owner of football club Shakhtar Donetsk — who is he?

Salvador Allende (26 June 1908 - 11 September 1973) was a Chilean socialist politician who served as the 29th president of Chile from 1970 until his suicide in 1973.

Gilded Age: Era of US history from the 1870s to the late 1890s.

Hatshepsut: Pharaoh of Egypt from 1479 to 1458 BC.

Hillsborough disaster: Fatal crowd crush during 1989 FA Cup semi-final. The Hillsborough disaster was a fatal crowd crush at a football match at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield, South Yorkshire, England, on 15 April 1989.

Jérôme Bonaparte: King of Westphalia from 1807 to 1813.

Khazars: Historical semi-nomadic Turkic ethnic group.
The son of a former Greek prime minister himself, who has led Greece's centre-right governing party since 2016 and served as PM since 2019?

An economist born in Hefei who rose through the Communist Youth League, he served as China's Premier from 2013 to 2023 — who was he?
Li Keqiang: Premier of China from 2013 to 2023. Born in Hefei, Anhui province, Li rose through the ranks in the Communist Youth League of China, serving as its first secretary from 1993 to 1998.

This Scottish politician led the Scottish National Party and served as First Minister from 2014 to 2023, after training as a solicitor and once stepping aside in a leadership race to back Alex Salmond — who is she?
Nicola Sturgeon: First Minister of Scotland from 2014 to 2023. Born in Ayrshire, Sturgeon is a law graduate of the University of Glasgow.
An English farmer-turned-soldier, he became a leading advocate for the 1649 execution of Charles I and then ruled as Lord Protector until his death in 1658 — who was he?

Trajan: Roman emperor from AD 98 to 117.

Velvet Revolution: Democratization process in Czechoslovakia in 1989.
This Chinese diplomat served as ambassador to Japan before becoming Minister of Foreign Affairs and later director of the Communist Party's Central Foreign Affairs Commission Office — who is he?

Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four. Thomas Carlyle (4 December 1795 – 5 February 1881) was a Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four. It is particularly useful in handling structured data, i.e., data incorporating relations among entities and variables.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
Marie Curie is a physicist. Curie was born in Warsaw, Russian Empire, where she studied at the clandestine Flying University and began her practical scientific training.
Which of these is a chemist?
Alfred Nobel is a chemist. Alfred Bernhard Nobel ( noh-BEL; Swedish: [ˈǎlːfrɛd nʊˈbɛlː]; 21 October 1833 – 10 December 1896) was a Swedish chemist, inventor, engineer, and businessman.
What is the atomic number of Fermium?
Fermium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Fm and atomic number 100.
In what year was Neil Armstrong born?
Neil Armstrong: Armstrong was born and raised near Wapakoneta, Ohio.
In what year did Karl Marx die?
Karl Marx: Born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia, Marx earned a doctoral degree in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841.
In what year was Argon discovered?
Argon is a chemical element; it has symbol Ar and atomic number 18.
Which company manufactures Consolidated B-24 Liberator?
Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control
Consolidated B-24 Liberator: North American Aviation. The Consolidated B-24 Liberator is an American heavy bomber, designed by Consolidated Aircraft of San Diego, California.
Cro-Magnon: France. Cro-Magnons produced Upper Palaeolithic cultures, the first major one being the Aurignacian, which was succeeded by the Gravettian by 30,000 years ago.
Who is credited with discovering Circinus?
Circinus: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Circinus is a small, faint constellation in the southern sky, first defined in 1756 by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille.
Who is credited with discovering Citric acid?
Citric acid: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Citric acid is an organic compound with the formula C6H8O7.
Who is credited with discovering Helium?
Helium: Pierre Janssen. Helium (from Ancient Greek: ἥλιος, romanized: helios, lit. 'sun') is a chemical element; it has symbol He and atomic number 2.
Russell Crowe stars in this 2001 Ron Howard film about a Nobel Prize-winning mathematician's struggle with schizophrenia, based on Sylvia Nasar's biography. What's the title?
A Beautiful Mind (film) is a 2001 American biographical drama film about the mathematician John Nash who won a Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.
Sometimes called emotional blindness, this neuropsychological condition involves trouble identifying or describing one's own feelings, and appears in about half of autistic people. What is it?
Alexithymia (-), also called emotional blindness, is a neuropsychological phenomenon characterized by difficulties processing or describing one's emotions.
This joint region where the foot meets the leg comprises three joints built from the talus, tibia, and fibula, enabling the foot's up-and-down flexing motions — what body part is it?
Ankle is the area where the foot and the leg meet.
Named from Greek words for 'even' and 'toe,' this mammal order bears its weight equally on two of its five toes, unlike its odd-toed counterpart — what order is it?
Artiodactyla (from Ancient Greek rtios 'even' and dktylos 'finger, toe') is an order of placental mammals.
Facing a shortage of staff, this American lawyer volunteered himself as chief prosecutor at the Einsatzgruppen trial at Nuremberg and later championed an International Criminal Court — who was he?
Ben Ferencz (March 11, 1920 - April 7, 2023) was an American lawyer.

This semi-solid tissue inside the spongy portions of bones serves as the primary site of new blood cell production in birds and mammals, making up roughly 5% of an adult human's body mass — what tissue is it?
Bone marrow is a semi-solid tissue found within the spongy (also known as cancellous) portions of bones.

What suborder of orthopteran insects — its Latin name meaning 'chisel-bearing,' after the stout shape of its members' egg-laying organs — includes grasshoppers, ground-hoppers, and pygmy mole crickets?
Caelifera are a suborder of orthopteran insects. The latter should not be confused with the mole crickets (Gryllotalpidae), which belong to the other Orthopteran suborder Ensifera.
Named for the whisker-like barbels many species sport, these scaleless ray-finned fish include some of the largest freshwater giants in Southeast Asia and Eurasia — name this diverse group of fish?
Catfish are a diverse group of ray-finned fish of the order Siluriformes (historically Nematognathi).
This insect family, known as the 'true' members of its group, contains roughly 3,400 species worldwide, distinct from just two species in a smaller sister family. What family is it?

Cicadidae is one of two families of cicadas, with about 3,400 species in over 520 genera worldwide; it contains most living cicada species, except for the two belonging to its sister taxon, the Tettigarctidae.

Serving as personal doctor to a superstar singer on the day of his 2009 death, this physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter over the misuse of a surgical anesthetic as a sleep aid — who is he?
Conrad Murray (born February 19, 1953) is a Grenadian-born American former physician convicted for his role in the death of American singer and dancer Michael Jackson.
First created in 1994 and named for the German city where it was made, this synthetic element with atomic number 110 sits below platinum on the periodic table — what's it called?
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Ds and atomic number 110.
Native to western North America, this towering conifer is also nicknamed Oregon pine or Columbian pine, though it isn't truly a pine at all — which tree?
Douglas fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii) is an evergreen conifer species in the pine family, Pinaceae.
Not a single disease but a syndrome of overall brain dysfunction with many possible causes, this term's Greek roots literally mean 'brain suffering' — what is it called?
Encephalopathy (from Ancient Greek (enkphalos) 'brain' and (pthos) 'suffering') is any disorder or disease of the brain, especially chronic degenerative conditions.
Known for filling pillows and blankets as well as lining the wings of birds, what are these soft, complex integumentary structures called?
Feather are epidermal growths that form a distinctive outer covering, or plumage, on both avian (bird) and some non-avian dinosaurs and other archosaurs.
Alongside co-founding a file-sharing site, this Swedish entrepreneur also started an internet service provider and web-hosting firm called PRQ — who is he?
Fredrik Neij (born 27 April 1978), alias TiAMO, is the co-founder of The Pirate Bay, and the Swedish Internet service provider and web hosting company PRQ.
The largest and outermost of the three hip muscles, this one shapes the buttocks and helps keep the human trunk upright — what muscle is it?
Gluteus maximus is the main extensor muscle of the hip in humans.

In 1896 this English physician dosed himself with mescaline and wrote one of the first public reports of the trip; he also co-wrote English's first medical textbook on homosexuality and coined the term 'narcissism' — who was he?
Havelock Ellis (2 February 1859 - 8 July 1939) was an English physician, eugenicist, writer, progressive intellectual and social reformer who studied human sexuality.
Found from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego across roughly 375 species, the males of this American bird family boast the most diverse plumage colors of any birds — what are they?
Hummingbird are birds native to the Americas and comprise the biological family Trochilidae.
An ISO standard defines it as "a new or changed entity, realizing or redistributing value" — and it's related to, but not the same as, invention. What word are we after?
Innovation is the practical implementation of ideas that result in the creation or improvements of goods or services.
This German polymath wrote The Sorrows of Young Werther and essays on botany, anatomy, and color theory—he's the most influential writer in the German language. Who was he?
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (28 August 1749 - 22 March 1832) was a German polymath who is widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language.
Which German engineer and economist founded the World Economic Forum in 1971 and chaired it until stepping down in 2025?
Klaus Schwab (born 30 March 1938) is a German mechanical engineer, economist, and founder of the World Economic Forum (WEF).
Viruses muddy its definition, and it might exist beyond Earth in unfamiliar forms — but on this planet it fills air, water and soil, even harsh niches of extremophiles. What is it?
Life is the capacity, in matter, for processes such as cell signaling, homeostasis, metabolism, cell growth, adaptation, response to stimuli, and reproduction.
This alpha-amino acid, a building block for many proteins, carries a side chain that stays partially charged at the body's normal pH, classifying it among the basic amino acids — what is it?
Lysine (symbol Lys or K) is an -amino acid that is a precursor to many proteins.

These aquatic insects carry ancient traits from the first flying insects — long tails and wings that won't fold flat — and their water-dwelling young are a living signal of clean, unpolluted streams; what bug is this?
Mayfly (also up-winged flies or up-wing flies, or drake-flies in the UK; shadflies or fishflies in northern U.S.
Also called selective sound sensitivity syndrome, this disorder causes specific everyday sounds to trigger intense, disproportionate emotional and physiological distress — what is it?
Misophonia (or selective sound sensitivity syndrome) is a disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds or their associated stimuli, or cues.
Found from Africa to Southeast Asia, this snake genus contains the 'true cobras' as opposed to look-alikes like the king cobra — which genus?
Naja is a genus of venomous elapid snakes commonly known as cobras (or "true cobras").
What organic molecule, composed of a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar, and a phosphate group, serves as the basic building block of both DNA and RNA?
Nucleotide are organic molecules composed of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate.
This rare silvery-white metal, discovered in 1802 and named after a newly found asteroid, is part of the six-element platinum group and has the lowest melting point among them. What element is it?
Palladium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Pd and atomic number 46.
Fill in the blank: “____ (born 12 January 1971) is a Danish convicted murderer and former entrepreneur.”

Peter Madsen (born 12 January 1971) is a Danish convicted murderer and former entrepreneur. Peter Langkjær Madsen (Danish: [ˈpʰe̝ˀtɐ ˈlɑŋˌkʰeˀɐ̯ ˈmæsn̩]; born 12 January 1971) is a Danish convicted murderer and former entrepreneur.
Reaching 30 to 50 meters tall and mostly found near rivers and wetlands, this tree genus's hybrid form has proven so tolerant of urban pollution it lines the streets of London — what's the genus?
Platanus is a genus consisting of a small number of tree species.

Found below the bladder with the urethra passing through it, this male reproductive gland acts as a mechanical switch between urination and ejaculation, and produces fluid that becomes part of semen — name the gland?
Prostate is an accessory gland of the male reproductive system and a muscle-driven mechanical switch between urination and ejaculation.

The largest of the true foxes and the most widely distributed carnivore on Earth, it spread alongside human settlement so successfully that, after being introduced to Australia, it landed on the list of the world's 100 worst invasive species. Which animal is it?
Red fox (Vulpes vulpes) is the largest of the true foxes, and the most widely distributed member of the order Carnivora.
Enforcing memory safety without a garbage collector through something called a 'borrow checker,' this general-purpose language blends functional and object-oriented paradigms — which language?
Rust (programming language) is a general-purpose programming language which emphasizes performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety.
This taxonomic order groups cephalopods distinguished by having ten arms instead of eight — what order is it?
Sepiida is an order of ten-armed cephalopods.
Found throughout the nightshade family — including in potato leaves, fruit, and tubers — this saponin-family toxin doubles as the plant's own natural pesticide. What compound is it?
Solanine is a glycoalkaloid poison found in species of the nightshade family within the genus Solanum, such as the potato (Solanum tuberosum).
In the equation 5 − 2 = 3, this is the operation being performed — which one is it?
Subtraction (which is signified by the minus sign) is one of the four arithmetic operations along with addition, multiplication and division.

This family of marine and freshwater fish can inflate themselves dramatically, revealing thin spines that stay hidden against their skin until they puff up — unlike their spinier, porcupine-like relatives — name this fish family?
Tetraodontidae is a family of marine and freshwater fish in the order Tetraodontiformes.

Stretching from the base of the skull down to the lower back and out to each shoulder blade, this large paired muscle supports the arm and moves the scapula in three distinct ways — what's the muscle?
Trapezius is a large paired trapezoid-shaped surface muscle that extends longitudinally from the occipital bone to the lower thoracic vertebrae of the spine and laterally to the spine of the scapula.
Mammals, birds, amphibians, fish, and reptiles all belong to this subphylum of animals, united by a backbone and a braincase — what is it?
Vertebrate are animals with a vertebral column and a cranium.
Marketed under names like Rompun, this veterinary sedative and alpha-2 adrenergic agonist is often combined with ketamine for animal anesthesia and used as an emetic in cats — what is it?

Xylazine is a structural analog of clonidine and an 2-adrenergic receptor agonist, sold under many trade names worldwide, most notably the Bayer brand name Rompun, as well as Anased, Sedazine and Chanazine.
Known by the common name yarrow, this pungent, fernleaved plant in the daisy family is used in traditional medicine and as livestock feed — what is its scientific name?
Achillea millefolium: Species of plant. Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
A former IMF economist, this politician has served as President of Ivory Coast since 2010 after earlier stints as the country's prime minister in the early 1990s — who is he?
Alassane Ouattara: President of Ivory Coast since 2010. Ouattara became the president of the Rally of the Republicans (RDR), an Ivorian political party, in 1999.
Native to the Americas, this plant is better known by its common names common ragweed, annual ragweed, or low ragweed — what is its scientific name?
Ambrosia artemisiifolia: Species of flowering plant in the daisy family.

Named from Greek words meaning "unlike other shrimp," this extinct arthropod from the Burgess Shale had swimming flaps, big compound eyes and grasping frontal appendages, reaching over a foot long — which prehistoric predator?
Anomalocaris: Extinct genus of cambrian radiodont.
Its guanidino group serves as the biological precursor for nitric oxide production, and this amino acid earned the one-letter code 'R' purely for phonetic reasons — what is it?
Arginine: Amino acid. Arginine is the amino acid with the formula (H2N)(HN)CN(H)(CH2)3CH(NH2)CO2H.
This broad category of technology uses machines and predetermined rules to reduce the need for human intervention in factories, boilers, and telephone switching — what is it?
Automation: Use of various control systems for operating equipment.
Spurred by the 1980 failure of Operation Eagle Claw, this American tiltrotor blends a helicopter's vertical takeoff with a turboprop's long-range cruise — what aircraft is it?
Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey: Military transport tiltrotor.

A French child prodigy who wrote a treatise on conic sections at 16, then built one of the first mechanical calculators and traded letters with Fermat that helped birth probability theory — who was he?
Typically housed in the head near the organs for vision, hearing, and smell, this organ processes thought and cognition while coordinating muscle activity — which organ?
Brain: Organ central to the nervous system.
Discovered in 1817 simultaneously by two German chemists as an impurity in zinc carbonate, this soft silvery-white metal shares chemical traits with zinc and mercury — which element?
Cadmium: Chemical element with atomic number 48 (Cd)
Called the 'father of modern taxonomy,' which Swedish biologist formalized the two-name system for naming living things and was later ennobled as von Linné?
Carl Linnaeus: Swedish biologist and physician (1707–1778)
First flown in 1955 as a tricycle-gear evolution of an earlier taildragger model, this four-seat high-wing aircraft is the most-produced plane in history — which model is it?
Cessna 172: Propeller driven single engine aircraft.

Most often documented in boxers and football players, this neurodegenerative disease is linked to repeated blows to the head and can worsen into dementia — what's its name, usually shortened to three letters?
Chronic traumatic encephalopathy: Neurodegenerative disease caused by head injury.
Native to tropical Africa and Asia, this plant genus produces caffeine-rich seeds that are roasted and brewed into one of the world's most valuable traded commodities — which genus?
Found only in placental mammals, this roughly four-inch bundle of 200 to 300 million nerve fibers is the brain's largest white-matter structure, linking its left and right hemispheres — what is it?
Corpus callosum: White matter tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.
Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, this disorder coats the lungs and other organs in thick mucus, inviting repeated bacterial infections — what genetic condition is it?
Cystic fibrosis: Genetic disorder affecting mostly the lungs.

Doctors once spotted this endocrine condition by its three Ps — polydipsia, polyuria, and polyphagia, or excessive thirst, urination, and hunger — all tracing back to trouble with insulin. Which disease is it?
Diabetes: Group of endocrine diseases characterized by high blood sugar levels.

Aristotle's Poetics contrasted this performance-based mode with the epic and the lyrical, and its name comes from a Greek word meaning "deed" or "act" — the two-masks symbol marks its split into comedy and tragedy. What is it?
Drama: Artwork intended for performance; formal type of literature.
Named for the large trunk-like proboscis of its males, this giant oceangoing pinniped can weigh up to 4,000 kilograms and was once hunted nearly to extinction for lamp oil. What animal is it?
Elephant seal: Genus of aquatic carnivores.
Sold under the brand name Nexium, this proton pump inhibitor treats acid reflux by blocking an enzyme in the stomach's acid-producing cells — what is it?
Esomeprazole: Medication which reduces stomach acid.
While its deciduous neighbors drop everything and go bare for winter, this kind of plant keeps its foliage green and working all year round — what's the botanical term?
Evergreen: Plant that has leaves in all seasons.
Spending 36 years at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory contributing to America's robotic space missions, which Iranian-American scientist later advised high-tech startups after retiring in 2016?
Only chefs with three-plus years of rigorous training may legally prepare this potentially lethal Japanese pufferfish dish, whose poison is tetrodotoxin — what is it?
Recognized as the world's longest ray-finned fish, this ribbon-shaped, silvery-blue deep-sea creature is often blamed for sea-serpent legends — which fish?
Giant oarfish: Species of oceanic ray-finned fish.
Descended from medieval hunting dogs once used to take down bears, boar, and deer for German nobility, this breed ties with the Irish Wolfhound as one of the world's two largest — which breed is it?
Great Dane: German breed of dog. The Great Dane is a German breed of large mastiff-sighthound, which descends from hunting dogs of the Middle Ages used to hunt bears, wild boar, and deer.
This German-American physicist won a 1967 Nobel Prize for explaining how a nuclear cycle powers heavy stars, after heading the Theoretical Division at Los Alamos during World War II — who is he?
In this condition, part of the stomach slips upward through the diaphragm into the chest, often triggering acid reflux, heartburn, or trouble swallowing — what is it?
Hiatal hernia: Entrance of abdominal organs into the middle chest through the diaphragm.
Also called prussic acid, this toxic, flammable liquid with the formula HCN boils just above room temperature and serves as an industrial precursor to plastics and mining chemicals — what is it?
Native to the subcontinent, the male of this bird species is called a peacock and sports a fan-shaped crest with a dazzling train of eyespot feathers used in courtship — which species?
Indian peafowl: Species of bird. The Indian peafowl (Pavo cristatus), also known as the common peafowl, or blue peafowl, is a species of peafowl native to the Indian subcontinent.
Awarded a gas-attack Iron Cross in WWI before sharing the 1925 Nobel with Gustav Hertz for the laws of how an electron strikes an atom — who was this German-American physicist?
This Hungarian-American polymath helped build the mathematical framework of quantum physics and codified ideas from game theory to cellular automata — who was he?
John von Neumann: Hungarian and American mathematician and physicist (1903–1957)
A biologist and botanist married four times — her last husband directed the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos lab — she was played by Emily Blunt in a 2023 film. Who was she?
A hybrid of the citron and the bitter orange, this small evergreen tree may have first appeared in northeastern India, and its fruit's juice is about 5–6% citric acid — what is it?

This anatomic form of lung infection causes inflammatory fluid to consolidate across an entire continuous section of one lung, and in children shows up instead as a rounded pattern due to immature air-pore connections — what is it?
Lobar pneumonia: Lung infection. It is one of three anatomic classifications of pneumonia (the other being bronchopneumonia and atypical pneumonia).
A field of artificial intelligence built on statistics and optimization, it develops algorithms that learn from data and handle unseen examples without being explicitly programmed — what is it?
Machine learning: Subset of artificial intelligence. Statistics and mathematical optimisation methods compose the foundations of machine learning.

In 1835 this Scottish polymath and Caroline Herschel became the first female Honorary Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, and she signed first on John Stuart Mill's 1866 petition for women's suffrage — who was she?

Diagnosed when a person has at least three of five red flags -- including abdominal obesity and high blood pressure -- this cluster of conditions raises the risk of heart disease and diabetes in about a quarter of US adults. What is it?
Metabolic syndrome: Cluster of diseases occurring with obesity.
This industry extracts everything from coal and gemstones to rock salt and gravel from the Earth, but is also linked to land degradation and habitat loss — what is it?
Mining: Extraction of valuable minerals or other geological materials from the Earth.
This contagious, vaccine-preventable viral disease is best known for causing painful swelling of the glands beside the jaw — its hallmark symptom. What is it?
Mumps: Human disease caused by paramyxovirus.
Discovered in 1885 by Carl Auer von Welsbach, this rare-earth element tarnishes quickly in air and produces pink, purple, and yellow compounds when oxidized — which element, atomic number 60?
Neodymium: Chemical element with atomic number 60 (Nd)
This Turkish-born American economist, a Harvard-trained NYU professor, earned lasting fame as one of the few who foresaw the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis. Who is he?
Common in adolescents during growth spurts, this condition causes a painful bump just below the knee from inflammation where the patellar ligament attaches to the shinbone — what is it?

Osgood–Schlatter disease: Inflammation of the patellar ligament. Osgood–Schlatter disease (OSD) is inflammation of the patellar ligament at the tibial tuberosity (apophysitis) usually affecting adolescents during growth spurts.
This cream-skinned root vegetable, a cousin of the carrot and parsley, actually grows sweeter in flavor after a winter frost — what is it?
Parsnip: Root vegetable in the flowering plant family Apiaceae.
Called the 'father of transplantation,' this Brazilian-born biologist won a 1960 Nobel for his work on acquired immune tolerance and graft rejection — who was he?
Known as the Scots pine in Britain, this Eurasian conifer is identifiable by its blue-green needles and orange-red bark — which species?
Pinus sylvestris: Species of conifer. Pinus sylvestris is a species of tree in the pine family Pinaceae that is native to Eurasia.
Also known as niter or saltpeter, this compound is a key ingredient of traditional gunpowder and gives cured meats their reddish color — what is it?
Potassium nitrate: Chemical compound. Potassium nitrate is a chemical compound with a sharp, salty, bitter taste and the chemical formula KNO3.
The earliest vertebrates known to achieve powered flight, these warm-blooded Mesozoic reptiles had wings stretched from ankle to a dramatically lengthened fourth finger — what were they called?
Pterosaur: Extinct order of flying reptiles.

A pioneer in optical character recognition and speech synthesis, this futurist inventor received the National Medal of Technology from President Clinton in 1999 for his outlook on AI and life extension — who is he?
Ray Kurzweil: American computer scientist, author and futurist (born 1948)
Often called the first modern chemist, which 17th-century Anglo-Irish natural philosopher described the inverse relationship between a gas's pressure and volume in a law that bears his name?
Named for the genus of the Atlantic salmon, this family of cold-water fish also includes trout, char, and grayling — what family is it?

Discovered in 1817 by Jöns Jacob Berzelius and named after the moon because of its resemblance to an element named for the Earth, this semiconductor finds use in glassmaking, pigments, and photocells — what element is it?
Selenium: Chemical element with atomic number 34 (Se)
The only species in its genus, this cosmopolitan pelagic fish from the mackerel family can grow past a metre long and matters hugely to global fisheries — which species?
Skipjack tuna: Species of fish. The skipjack tuna (Katsuwonus pelamis) is a perciform fish in the tuna family, Scombridae, and is the only member of the genus Katsuwonus.
Sold under the brand name Aldactone, this diuretic medication treats heart failure and acne, and is also used to block testosterone's effects during feminizing hormone therapy — what is it?
NATO calls it 'Frogfoot' but its Soviet designers named it after the rook; this subsonic twin-engine jet first flew in 1975 to give close air support to ground forces — which aircraft?
Sukhoi Su-25: Soviet attack aircraft introduced 1978.
This Japanese immunologist shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with James P. Allison for identifying the PD-1 protein — who is he?
Tasuku Honjo: Japanese immunologist and Nobel laureate (born 1942)
Nicknamed thunderflies, these minute fringe-winged insects are too feeble for normal flight, so they fly using a 'clap and fling' trick that conjures lift from tiny vortices. What are they?
Thrips: Order of insects. Thrips are a functionally diverse group; many of the known species are fungivorous.
Botanically a perennial with an elongated trunk, this form isn't a single family — palms, ferns, and bamboos all independently grew tall stems to win at chasing sunlight. What is it?
Tree: Perennial woody plant with elongated trunk.
Medically called micturition or voiding, this voluntary process happens up to seven times a day in a healthy adult — what is it?
Urination: Release of urine from the urinary bladder.
Comprising the mons pubis, labia, clitoris, and vaginal opening, these external structures of the female genitalia are supplied by the pudendal arteries. What is this collectively called?
Vulva: External genitalia of the female mammal. The folds of the outer and inner labia provide a double layer of protection for the vagina (which leads to the uterus).
Nicknamed 'Superman syndrome,' this genetic condition gives males an extra Y chromosome, often extra height but usually normal fertility — which one?
XYY syndrome: Genetic condition in which a male has an extra Y chromosome.

Radium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for radium is Ra. Radium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ra and atomic number 88.

Giancarlo Esposito: Giancarlo Giuseppe Alessandro Esposito (Italian: [dʒaŋˈkarlo dʒuˈzɛppe alesˈsandro eˈspɔːzito]; born April 26, 1958) is an American actor and director.
